claim: Low-intensity transcranial ultrasound (TUS) can non-invasively modulate human neural activity.
source: Low-intensity transcranial ultrasound (TUS) can non-invasively modulate human neural activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general premise of the study.

claim: A low-intensity 500 kHz TUS transducer was coupled to a transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) coil.
source: A low-intensity 500 kHz TUS transducer was coupled to a transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) coil.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup used in the study.

claim: TMS was delivered 10 ms before the end of TUS to the left M1 hotspot of the first dorsal interosseous muscle.
source: TMS was delivered 10 ms before the end of TUS to the left M1 hotspot of the first dorsal interosseous muscle.
evidence: This describes the timing protocol used in the experiments.

claim: TUS safely suppressed TMS-elicited motor cortical activity, with longer sonication durations and shorter duty cycles when delivered in a blocked paradigm.
source: TUS safely suppressed TMS-elicited motor cortical activity, with longer sonication durations and shorter duty cycles when delivered in a blocked paradigm.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: TUS increased GABAA-mediated short-interval intracortical inhibition.
source: TUS increased GABAA-mediated short-interval intracortical inhibition and decreased reaction time on visuomotor task but not when controlled with TUS at near-somatosensory threshold intensity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by paired-pulse TMS data.

claim: TUS decreased reaction time on visuomotor task but not when controlled with TUS at near-somatosensory threshold intensity.
source: TUS increased GABAA-mediated short-interval intracortical inhibition and decreased reaction time on visuomotor task but not when controlled with TUS at near-somatosensory threshold intensity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral task data.

claim: Low-intensity TUS is a promising noninvasive brain stimulation technique actively being studied for its ability to reversibly modulate mammalian brain activity.
source: Low-intensity transcranial ultrasound (TUS) is a promising noninvasive brain stimulation technique actively being studied for its ability to reversibly modulate mammalian brain activity (Fomenko et al., 2018; Naor et al., 2016; Tyler et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: By focusing the propagation of acoustic waves through the skull, a higher degree of spatial specificity and deeper targeting can be achieved over other noninvasive stimulation methods such as transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and transcranial direct-current stimulation.
source: By focusing the propagation of acoustic waves through the skull, a higher degree of spatial specificity and deeper targeting can be achieved over other noninvasive stimulation methods such as transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and transcranial direct-current stimulation (Fomenko and Lozano, 2019; Pasquinelli et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: It remains unknown how varying the sonication parameters (i.e.: sonication duration, duty cycle, frequency) affects the magnitude and direction of neural activity within human brain circuits.
source: although it remains unknown how varying the sonication parameters (i.e.: sonication duration, duty cycle, frequency) affects the magnitude and direction of neural activity within human brain circuits (Ai et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2016b; Legon et al., 2014; Sanguinetti et al., 2014).
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Published human experiments have demonstrated electrophysiological suppression of sensory-evoked potentials, task performance alteration, modulation of cortical oscillatory dynamics, and corresponding activation on fMRI.
source: To date, published human experiments have demonstrated electrophysiological suppression of sensory-evoked potentials, task performance alteration, modulation of cortical oscillatory dynamics, and corresponding activation on fMRI (Lee et al., 2016a; Legon et al., 2014; Mueller et al., 2014).
evidence: This summarizes prior findings in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Self-reported outcomes induced by TUS have included mood improvement, phosphene detection, and tactile limb sensations, when frontal, somatosensory, and occipital cortices were targeted, respectively.
source: Self-reported outcomes induced by TUS have included mood improvement (Hameroff et al., 2013), phosphene detection (Lee et al., 2016b; Schimek et al., 2020), and tactile limb sensations (Lee et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2016a), when frontal, somatosensory, and occipital cortices were targeted, respectively.
evidence: This summarizes prior findings in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Each study examined only a single set of stimulation parameters, and it is not known whether human neural circuits are more sensitive to titration of a particular parameter, nor whether a dose-response effect exists.
source: However, each study examined only a single set of stimulation parameters, and it is not known whether human neural circuits are more sensitive to titration of a particular parameter, nor whether a dose-response effect exists.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: Studies reported heterogeneous effects of TUS on targets such as the motor cortex, with some studies showing suppression of motor-evoked potentials (MEPs), and others demonstrating increased cortical excitability after prolonged sonication.
source: Furthermore, studies reported heterogeneous effects of TUS on targets such as the motor cortex, with some studies showing suppression of motor-evoked potentials (MEPs) (Legon et al., 2018a), and others demonstrating increased cortical excitability after prolonged sonication (Gibson et al., 2018).
evidence: This summarizes conflicting findings in prior literature, supported by citations.

claim: This is the first double-blinded study examining the effects of systematically varying sonication parameters of TUS applied to the primary motor cortex (M1) of healthy human participants.
source: Here, we describe the first double-blinded study examining the effects of systematically varying sonication parameters of TUS applied to the primary motor cortex (M1) of healthy human participants (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the novelty of the current study.

claim: Measurement of MEPs from TMS provides an objective and readily quantifiable measure of M1 excitability.
source: We tested the M1 because measurement of MEPs from TMS provides an objective and readily quantifiable measure of M1 excitability.
evidence: This justifies the choice of M1 as the target region based on established knowledge.

claim: The estimated intracranial intensity of TUS at basic parameters was calculated to correspond to ISPTA = 0.69 W/cm2, ISPPA = 2.32 W/cm2, and a mechanical index of 0.19.
source: At basic parameters, the estimated intracranial intensity of TUS at basic parameters was calculated to correspond to ISPTA = 0.69 W/cm2, ISPPA = 2.32 W/cm2, and a mechanical index of 0.19.
evidence: This provides quantitative characterization of the acoustic parameters used.

claim: The FDA cephalic acoustic exposure guidelines are defined as ISPTA ≤94 mW/cm2, and either MI ≤ 1.9 or derated ISPPA ≤ 190 W/cm2.
source: The FDA cephalic acoustic exposure guidelines are defined as ISPTA ≤94 mW/cm2, and either MI ≤ 1.9 or derated ISPPA ≤ 190 W/cm2 (Duck, 2007; United States Food and Drug Administration, 2017).
evidence: This cites regulatory guidelines for safety comparison.

claim: No subjects reported any adverse effects, but two (13%) participants reported a transient warm sensation at the sonication site after multiple experimental blocks.
source: No subjects reported any adverse effects, but two (13%) participants reported a transient warm sensation at the sonication site after multiple experimental blocks.
evidence: This reports safety outcomes from the study.

claim: Neurological examinations after each experimental visit were normal, supporting the safety profile of the current pulsing schemes.
source: Neurological examinations after each experimental visit were normal, supporting the safety profile of the current pulsing schemes.
evidence: This reports safety outcomes from the study.

claim: The probabilistic averaged map of the induced electromagnetic current across all participants (n = 16) confirmed that the M1 hand knob was effectively targeted with TMS.
source: The probabilistic averaged map of the induced electromagnetic current across all participants (n = 16) confirmed that the M1 hand knob was effectively targeted with TMS (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data and Figure 2A.

claim: The individual simulations of ultrasound propagation for each participant confirmed acoustic targeting of a portion of M1, as well as underlying corticospinal white matter.
source: Similarly, the individual simulations of ultrasound propagation for each participant confirmed acoustic targeting of a portion of M1, as well as underlying corticospinal white matter. (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The focal length within the −6 dB of the focus was 23 mm, and the focal width at half-maximum of our transducer was determined to be 6 mm.
source: The focal length within the −6 dB of the focus was 23 mm, and the focal width at half-maximum of our transducer was determined to be 6 mm (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by transducer characterization data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The mean TMS stimulator intensity required to generate a 0.5 mV MEP was 58% (range 50–80%).
source: The mean TMS stimulator intensity required to generate a 0.5 mV MEP was 58% (range 50–80%).
evidence: This reports a measurement from the experimental protocol.

claim: Basic parameters suppressed MEP amplitudes (0.33 ± 0.06 mV; n = 12) compared to active sham (0.63 ± 0.09 mV; n = 12; two-tailed paired t-test, t = 6.36, df = 11, p<0.001).
source: Basic parameters suppressed MEP amplitudes (0.33 ± 0.06 mV; n = 12) compared to active sham (0.63 ± 0.09 mV; n = 12; two-tailed paired t-test, t = 6.36, df = 11, p<0.001)
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: Basic parameters also suppressed mean MEP voltage (0.21 ± 0.04 mV; n = 4) compared to inactive sham (0.49 ± 0.09 mV; n = 4; two-tailed paired t-test, t = 5.41, df = 3, p=0.012).
source: and basic parameters also suppressed mean MEP voltage (0.21 ± 0.04 mV; n = 4) compared to inactive sham (0.49 ± 0.09 mV; n = 4; two-tailed paired t-test, t = 5.41, df = 3, p=0.012) (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical analysis, shown in Figure 4.

claim: Varying the duty cycle showed a significant effect on MEP amplitude (RM one-way ANOVA, F = 5.98, df = 15, p=0.015).
source: Varying the duty cycle showed a significant effect on MEP amplitude (RM one-way ANOVA, F = 5.98, df = 15, p=0.015).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: TUS at a duty cycle of 10% suppressed MEPs significantly (0.36 ± 0.06 mV; n = 16; t = 2.93, df = 15, adjusted p=0.027) compared to sham (0.63 ± 0.14 mV; n = 16).
source: Compared to sham (0.63 ± 0.14 mV; n = 16), post-hoc two-tailed paired t-tests with correction for multiple comparisons showed that TUS at a duty cycle of 10% suppressed MEPs significantly (0.36 ± 0.06 mV; n = 16; t = 2.93, df = 15, adjusted p=0.027).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: Sonication at 30% DC (0.48 ± 0.10 mV; n = 16; t = 2.08, df = 15, adjusted p=0.10) and 50% DC (0.44 ± 0.08 mV; n = 16; t = 2.12, df = 15, adjusted p=0.10) had no significant effect.
source: Sonication at 30% DC (0.48 ± 0.10 mV; n = 16; t = 2.08, df = 15, adjusted p=0.10) and 50% DC (0.44 ± 0.08 mV; n = 16; t = 2.12, df = 15, adjusted p=0.10) had no significant effect (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis, shown in Figure 5.

claim: Varying the sonication duration had a significant effect on MEP amplitude (RM one-way ANOVA, F = 15.12, df = 15, p<0.001).
source: Varying the sonication duration also had a significant effect on MEP amplitude (RM one-way ANOVA, F = 15.12, df = 15, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: Sonication for 0.4 s (0.47 ± 0.08 mV; n = 16; t = 4.29, df = 15, adjusted p=0.003) and 0.5 s (0.47 ± 0.11 mV; n = 16; t = 4.12, df = 15, adjusted p=0.004) showed significant suppression compared to sham (0.89 ± 0.13 mV; n = 16).
source: Post-hoc two-tailed paired t-tests with correction for multiple comparisons showed significant suppression compared to sham (0.89 ± 0.13 mV; n = 16) when sonicating for 0.4 s (0.47 ± 0.08 mV; n = 16; t = 4.29, df = 15, adjusted p=0.003), and 0.5 s (0.47 ± 0.11 mV; n = 16; t = 4.12, df = 15, adjusted p=0.004).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: Sonication for 0.1 s (0.87 ± 0.15 mV; n = 16; t = 0.28, df = 15, adjusted p=1.00), 0.2 s (0.84 ± 0.14 mV; n = 16; t = 0.73, df = 15, adjusted p=0.92), or 0.3 s (0.66 ± 0.11 mV; n = 16; t = 2.33, df = 15, adjusted p=0.12) was not significantly different from sham stimulation.
source: Sonication for 0.1 s (0.87 ± 0.15 mV; n = 16; t = 0.28, df = 15, adjusted p=1.00), 0.2 s (0.84 ± 0.14 mV; n = 16; t = 0.73, df = 15, adjusted p=0.92), or 0.3 s (0.66 ± 0.11 mV; n = 16; t = 2.33, df = 15, adjusted p=0.12) was not significantly different from sham stimulation.
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: Varying the PRF with fixed DC did not have a significant effect on evoked potentials (RM one-way ANOVA, F = 2.90, p=0.08).
source: Varying the PRF with fixed DC did not have a significant effect on evoked potentials (RM one-way ANOVA, F = 2.90, p=0.08).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: Varying the PRF with adjusted DC to ensure a fixed pulse duration did not have a significant effect on MEPs (RM one-way ANOVA, F = 1.22, p=0.31).
source: Similarly, varying the PRF with adjusted DC to ensure a fixed pulse duration did not have a significant effect on MEPs (RM one-way ANOVA, F = 1.22, p=0.31).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: Varying the duty cycle with interleaved trials showed a significant effect on MEP amplitudes (n = 16, F = 3.94, df = 15, p=0.02; RM one-way ANOVA).
source: Varying the duty cycle with interleaved trials (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) showed a significant effect on MEP amplitudes (n = 16, F = 3.94, df = 15, p=0.02; RM one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In interleaved trials, a DC of 10% (0.41 ± 0.05 mV; n = 16; t = 3.12, df = 15, adjusted p=0.020) significantly suppressed MEPs compared to sham (0.56 ± 0.06 mV; n = 16).
source: Compared to sham (0.56 ± 0.06 mV; n = 16), post-hoc two-tailed paired t-tests with correction for multiple comparisons showed that a DC of 10% (0.41 ± 0.05 mV; n = 16; t = 3.12, df = 15, adjusted p=0.020) significantly suppressed MEPs, while a DC of 30% (0.48 ± 0.05 mV; n = 16; t = 1.47, df = 15, adjusted p=0.35) and 50% (0.45 ± 0.07 mV; n = 16; t = 2.06, df = 15, adjusted p=0.14) did not.
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: Blocked variation of the DC showed a significant effect on MEP amplitudes (n = 16, F = 11.2, df = 15, p<0.0001; RM one-way ANOVA).
source: Blocked variation of the DC also showed a significant effect on MEP amplitudes (n = 16, F = 11.2, df = 15, p<0.0001; RM one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: In blocked trials, a DC of 10% (0.34 ± 0.04 mV; n = 16; t = 3.51, df = 15, adjusted p=0.010) and 30% (0.28 ± 0.05 mV; n = 16; t = 4.54, df = 15, adjusted p=0.002) significantly suppressed MEPs compared to sham (0.59 ± 0.07 mV; n = 16).
source: Compared to sham (0.59 ± 0.07 mV; n = 16), post-hoc two-tailed paired t-tests with correction for multiple comparisons showed that a DC of 10% (0.34 ± 0.04 mV; n = 16; t = 3.51, df = 15, adjusted p=0.010) and 30% (0.28 ± 0.05 mV; n = 16; t = 4.54, df = 15, adjusted p=0.002) significantly suppressed MEPs, while a DC of 50% (0.49 ± 0.06 mV; n = 16; t = 1.59, df = 15, adjusted p=0.297) had no significant effect.
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: Post-hoc analysis of individual trials showed no significant differences between early and late trials in the sham, 10%, 30%, or 50% conditions (n = 16, adjusted p=0.31, 0.31, 0.81, 0.81; paired t-tests).
source: Post-hoc analysis of individual trials (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) showed no significant differences between early and late trials in the sham, 10%, 30%, or 50% conditions (n = 16, adjusted p=0.31, 0.31, 0.81, 0.81; paired t-tests).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Randomly interleaving the pulse repetition frequency with constant DC parameters did not result in significant differences across conditions (n = 16, F = 2.24, df = 15, p=0.1226; RM one-way ANOVA).
source: Randomly interleaving the pulse repetition frequency with constant DC parameters did not result in significant differences across conditions (n = 16, F = 2.24, df = 15, p=0.1226; RM one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: Grouping PRF parameters in a blocked paradigm resulted in significant effects on MEP amplitudes (n = 16, df = 15, F = 14.0, p<0.001; RM one-way ANOVA).
source: However, grouping parameters in a blocked paradigm resulted in significant effects on MEP amplitudes (n = 16, df = 15, F = 14.0, p<0.001; RM one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: In blocked PRF trials with constant DC, a PRF of 200 Hz (0.56 ± 0.10 mV; n = 16; t = 4.43, df = 15, adjusted p=0.001), 500 Hz (0.50 ± 0.09 mV; n = 16; t = 5.29, df = 15, adjusted p<0.001), and 1000 Hz (0.37 ± 0.07 mV; n = 16; t = 5.53, df = 15, adjusted p<0.001) all significantly suppressed MEPs compared to sham (0.75 ± 0.10 mV; n = 16).
source: Compared to sham (0.75 ± 0.10 mV; n = 16), post-hoc two-tailed paired t-tests with correction for multiple comparisons showed that a PRF of 200 Hz (0.56 ± 0.10 mV; n = 16; t = 4.43, df = 15, adjusted p=0.001), 500 Hz (0.50 ± 0.09 mV; n = 16; t = 5.29, df = 15, adjusted p<0.001), and 1000 Hz (0.37 ± 0.07 mV; n = 16; t = 5.53, df = 15, adjusted p<0.001) all significantly suppressed MEPs.
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: Interleaving the pulse repetition frequency with adjusted DC parameters did not result in significant differences across conditions (n = 16, F = 0.50, df = 15, p=0.648; RM one-way ANOVA).
source: Interleaving the pulse repetition frequency with adjusted DC parameters did not result in significant differences across conditions (n = 16, F = 0.50, df = 15, p=0.648; RM one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: Grouping PRF parameters with adjusted DC in a blocked paradigm resulted in significant effects on MEP amplitudes (n = 16, df = 15, F = 9.39, p=0.003; RM one-way ANOVA).
source: However, grouping parameters in a blocked paradigm resulted in significant effects on MEP amplitudes (n = 16, df = 15, F = 9.39, p=0.003; RM one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: In blocked PRF trials with adjusted DC, a PRF of 200 Hz (0.50 ± 0.09 mV; n = 16; t = 3.49, df = 15, adjusted p=0.011), 500 Hz (0.45 ± 0.09 mV; n = 16; t = 5.33, df = 15, adjusted p<0.001), and 1000 Hz (0.42 ± 0.09 mV; n = 16; t = 3.16, df = 15, adjusted p=0.021) all significantly suppressed MEPs compared to sham (0.72 ± 0.11 mV; n = 16).
source: Compared to sham (0.72 ± 0.11 mV; n = 16), post-hoc two-tailed paired t-tests with correction for multiple comparisons showed that a PRF of 200 Hz (0.50 ± 0.09 mV; n = 16; t = 3.49, df = 15, adjusted p=0.011), 500 Hz (0.45 ± 0.09 mV; n = 16; t = 5.33, df = 15, adjusted p<0.001), and 1000 Hz (0.42 ± 0.09 mV; n = 16; t = 3.16, df = 15, adjusted p=0.021) all significantly suppressed MEPs.
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: During muscle contraction, active MEP amplitudes did not significantly differ between sham (7.65 ± 0.75 mV; n = 12) compared to TUS (7.79 ± 0.88 mV; n = 12; two-tailed paired t-test, t = 0.44, df = 11, p=0.67).
source: During muscle contraction, active MEP amplitudes did not significantly differ between sham (7.65 ± 0.75 mV; n = 12) compared to TUS (7.79 ± 0.88 mV; n = 12; two-tailed paired t-test, t = 0.44, df = 11, p=0.67).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: The silent period (SP) duration after sham (131 ± 10 ms; n = 12) did not significantly differ from TUS (138 ± 9 ms; n = 12; two-tailed paired t-test, t = 0.52, df = 11, p=0.61).
source: The silent period (SP) duration after sham (131 ± 10 ms; n = 12) did not significantly differ from TUS (138 ± 9 ms; n = 12; two-tailed paired t-test, t = 0.52, df = 11, p=0.61). (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis, shown in Figure 6.

claim: The mean TMS stimulator output required to produce a 1 mV MEP with sonication at basic parameters (78.8, range 55–97% MSO; n = 12) was significantly higher (mean of differences = +1.3%; n = 12; two-tailed paired t-test, t = 2.86, df = 11, p=0.02) than the output required to produce a 1 mV MEP under sham (77.4 range 57–99% MSO; n = 12).
source: Among all subjects, the mean TMS stimulator output required to produce a 1 mV MEP with sonication at basic parameters (78.8, range 55–97% MSO; n = 12) was significantly higher (mean of differences = +1.3%; n = 12; two-tailed paired t-test, t = 2.86, df = 11, p=0.02) than the output required to produce a 1 mV MEP under sham (77.4 range 57–99% MSO; n = 12) (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis, shown in Figure 7.

claim: Short-interval intracortical inhibition at 2 ms was significantly increased with TUS application at basic parameters (0.40 ± 0.07 ratio to TS; n = 12) compared to sham (0.60 ± 0.10 ratio to TS; n = 12; two-tailed paired t-test, t = 2.32, df = 11, p=0.038).
source: Short-interval intracortical iinhibition at 2 ms was significantly increased with TUS application at basic parameters (0.40 ± 0.07 ratio to TS; n = 12) compared to sham (0.60 ± 0.10 ratio to TS; n = 12; two-tailed paired t-test, t = 2.32, df = 11, p=0.038).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: Long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI) at 100 ms, short-interval intracortical facilitation (SICF) at 1.5 ms, SICF at 2.9, and intracortical facilitation (ICF) at 10 ms revealed no significant differences between sham and active TUS application time-locked to the first stimulus (n = 12; two-tailed t-tests, df = 11, p-values 0.91, 0.66, 0.75, 0.90, respectively).
source: Long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI) at 100 ms, short-interval intracortical facilitation (SICF) at 1.5 ms, SICF at 2.9, and intracortical facilitation (ICF) at 10 ms revealed no significant differences between sham and active TUS application time-locked to the first stimulus (n = 12; two-tailed t-tests, df = 11, p-values 0.91, 0.66, 0.75, 0.90, respectively).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: The pooled reaction time to the presentation of visual stimulus was significantly shorter with TUS applied at basic intensity and parameters (363 ± 68 ms; n = 12) compared to sham stimulation (521.57 ± 20 ms; n = 12; two-tailed paired t-test, t = 2.27, df = 11, p=0.04).
source: The pooled reaction time to the presentation of visual stimulus was significantly shorter with TUS applied at basic intensity and parameters (363 ± 68 ms; n = 12) compared to sham stimulation (521.57 ± 20 ms; n = 12; two-tailed paired t-test, t = 2.27, df = 11, p=0.04) (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical analysis, shown in Figure 8.

claim: In four additional subjects, the reaction times were not significantly different between TUS applied at 0.54 W/cm2 subthreshold intensity (305 ± 45 ms; n = 4) compared to basic 2.32 W/cm2 intensity (301 ± 44 ms; n = 4; two-tailed paired t-test, t = 2.68, df = 3, p=0.08).
source: In four additional subjects, the reaction times were not significantly different between TUS applied at 0.54 W/cm2 subthreshold intensity (305 ± 45 ms; n = 4) compared to basic 2.32 W/cm2 intensity (301 ± 44 ms; n = 4; two-tailed paired t-test, t = 2.68, df = 3, p=0.08).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference between application of TUS or sham in the mean total distance travelled, deviation scores, or time taken per trial (one-way, RM one-way ANOVA, p>0.05).
source: There was no significant difference between application of TUS or sham in the mean total distance travelled, deviation scores, or time taken per trial (one-way, RM one-way ANOVA, p>0.05).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: A recent systematic examination of TUS parameters in sheep showed that low duty cycles (<10%) and long sonication durations (~1 min) yielded suppressive effects on sensory-evoked potentials, while high duty cycles (>30%) and short sonication durations (<500 ms) were excitatory on the motor cortex.
source: A recent systematic examination of TUS parameters in sheep showed that low duty cycles (<10%) and long sonication durations (~1 min) yielded suppressive effects on sensory-evoked potentials, while high duty cycles (>30%) and short sonication durations (<500 ms) were excitatory on the motor cortex (Yoon et al., 2019)
evidence: This summarizes findings from prior literature, supported by citation.

claim: When delivered in blocked fashion, longer sonication durations, lower duty cycles, and all three PRFs tested yield effective suppression of TMS-elicited MEPs.
source: In summary, our findings suggest that when delivered in blocked fashion, longer sonication durations, lower duty cycles, and all three PRFs tested yield effective suppression of TMS-elicited MEPs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The trend toward greater suppression with increasing blocked PRF agree with recent literature, where higher PRF (1500 Hz) in combination with low duty cycles were found to be more effective than lower PRF (300 Hz) in neuromodulation of mouse motor cortex in vivo and in vitro.
source: The trend toward greater suppression with increasing blocked PRF agree with recent literature, where higher PRF (1500 Hz) in combination with low duty cycles were found to be more effective than lower PRF (300 Hz) in neuromodulation of mouse motor cortex in vivo (King et al., 2013) and in vitro (Manuel et al., 2020).
evidence: This compares the current findings to prior literature, supported by citations.

claim: Recent large animal studies reveal a bidirectional neuromodulation effects of varying TUS parameters.
source: Furthermore, recent large animal studies reveal a bidirectional neuromodulation effects of varying TUS parameters (Yoon et al., 2019).
evidence: This summarizes findings from prior literature, supported by citation.

claim: Interleaving different parameters in short succession may lead to spillover effects, due to the random order of parameter delivery.
source: As such, interleaving different parameters in short succession may lead to spillover effects, due to the random order of parameter delivery.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Non-linear effects were found in animal studies where randomized delivery of TUS parameters was studied, possibly related to non-linear piezoelectric accumulation across the neural membrane capacity under the Neuronal Bilayer Sonophore model.
source: From animal studies where randomized delivery of TUS parameters was studied, non-linear effects were found, possibly related to non-linear piezoelectric accumulation across the neural membrane capacity under the Neuronal Bilayer Sonophore model (Kim et al., 2014; Plaksin et al., 2014).
evidence: This summarizes findings from prior literature and proposes a mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: Excitatory or inhibitory changes in short-term plasticity may occur with repeated TUS stimulation, similar to those observed with repeated magnetic and electrical stimulation.
source: In addition, excitatory or inhibitory changes in short-term plasticity may occur with repeated TUS stimulation, similar to those observed with repeated magnetic (Watanabe et al., 2014) and electrical stimulation (Udupa et al., 2016).
evidence: This proposes a mechanism based on analogy to other stimulation modalities, supported by citations.

claim: Within each parameter condition, there was no significant difference between the magnitude of early and late trials, indicating no temporal accumulation of MEP-suppressive effects over blocks of 15 trials.
source: Within each parameter condition, we did not detect a significant difference between the magnitude of early and late trials and conclude that there is no temporal accumulation of MEP-suppressive effects over blocks of 15 trials, corresponding to a block length of approximately 90 s.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on post-hoc analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The suppression appears to be instantaneous, with effective parameters increasing the likelihood of generating a lower TMS-elicited MEP, but not potentiating the effect of a subsequent stimulation.
source: Instead, the suppression appears to be instantaneous, with effective parameters increasing the likelihood of generating a lower TMS-elicited MEP, but not potentiating the effect of a subsequent stimulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.
